messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun had always seen the city skyline from his tiny office cubicle, sketching user flows while a soft hum of air‑conditioning filled the room. The typhoon that slammed the coast three months ago had come without warning. He was on the balcony of his apartment, clutching a coffee mug, when the wind slammed the shutters shut and a gust of rain turned the balcony’s concrete into a slick, unsteady surface. A neighbor, older and frail, slipped, and Arjun felt his own body snap as the earth seemed to tilt beneath him. The water surged up the walls, and in the brief, dizzying seconds he heard the distant crash of a window and the wet slap of a hand reaching for the railing. The world collapsed into a sharp, roaring noise, and he was thrown into the cold, flooded hallway of his own building, where the smell of rain and metal met the sudden, sickening heaviness in his chest. When Arjun wakes each morning, a throbbing ache in his neck and a vague feeling of being unwell sit at the edge of his awareness, as if his body is still trembling from that night. These physical sensations are the first thing that bring the memory back: a flash of the balcony’s slick, gray surface, the sharp taste of salt in the air, and the ghost of a scream echoing over the pounding rain. He remembers the way his heart hammered, the way the wind seemed to push him backward, and the moment he felt a sudden, intense nausea that left his stomach in knots. The taste of rain, so vivid that he can almost smell the wet concrete, lingers each time the memory returns, and sometimes he feels a wave of raw emotion—fear, helplessness—surging without any clear image to latch onto. The memory is so extreme that he questions its authenticity, feeling as though the story is unreal, a phantom that refuses to die even as he tries to keep it locked away. The haunting recollection of that night has seeped into his trust of others. Arjun has begun to think that people are unreliable, that when disaster strikes, strangers may flee just as fast as they appear. The terror he felt, the feeling of being abandoned in a chaotic moment, has also sharpened his sense of isolation; the people who were there, if any, were unhelpful or too overwhelmed to offer assistance. The idea that he no longer belongs anywhere has settled over him like a heavy coat, and he finds himself questioning his connection to his friends, his coworkers, and even the digital communities he once found comfort in. The memory’s vividness has reinforced these thoughts, making him more skeptical of others’ intentions and more convinced that he is alone in the world. Physical discomfort in Arjun’s neck and the lingering sense of sickness now amplify his mistrust and sense of isolation. The first time he feels a sharp pain in his neck after sitting too long at his desk, he immediately thinks of that night’s chaotic movements, and the dread that people might be careless or unreliable spikes. He begins to withdraw, turning down social invitations from coworkers, and chooses to stay in his office rather than engage in team lunch or collaborative brainstorming. Each time he avoids a group meeting, his feeling of being unwell sharpens, as if the body is reminding him of that earlier, uncontrolled moment. This avoidance deepens his isolation, and the cycle of mistrust and discomfort feeds into one another. Because Arjun distrusts people, he now finds himself avoiding elevators and crowded hallways in his building, choosing instead to walk up the stairs—an action that strains his neck and leaves him feeling light‑headed. His isolation at work keeps him from seeking help or sharing his discomfort, and the continued avoidance of people and crowds amplifies his physical symptoms. The resulting pain and illness reinforce his belief that people are unreliable, and his isolation feels more profound. The loop tightens as he feels that every attempt to engage with others is met with his own discomfort and the echo of the storm’s terror. Now, sitting on the edge of a therapist’s chair, Arjun feels the familiar weight in his neck, the sudden sting of nausea, and the overwhelming sense that he is alone in the world. The urge to avoid anyone who might remind him of that night pulls at him, but he also feels a glimmer of hope: that speaking about the storm, about the taste of rain and the sharp, unreal memories, might begin to loosen the cycle that has bound him to distrust, isolation, and pain. The most frightening thought is that another storm—real or imagined—will strike again, unleashing the same chain of triggers and thoughts. Yet he is also, quietly, hoping that with guidance, he can learn to separate the echoes of that night from his everyday life, to reconnect with colleagues, and to feel a sense of belonging once more.
